tx.t: Today I will explain how the human heart works. The heart has four chambers: two at the top, called atria, and two at the bottom, called ventricles.
At rest, the adult heart beats between sixty and one hundred times every minute. Over a day, that adds up to roughly one hundred thousand beats.
The heart pumps about five litres of blood around the body every minute. The heart of an adult weighs only about three hundred grams, and it is about the size of a clenched fist.
Regular exercise makes the heart stronger, so it can pump more blood with each beat.

tx.t: Today we are going to look at Antarctica, the coldest continent. About ninety-eight per cent of Antarctica is covered in ice.

The lowest temperature ever recorded on Earth, minus eighty-nine degrees Celsius, was measured there at Vostok Station in nineteen eighty-three. The ice contains about seventy per cent of the world's fresh water.

No people are native to Antarctica. Only scientists live there, and their numbers change with the seasons. The Antarctic Treaty of nineteen fifty-nine, signed by twelve countries, says that the continent can be used only for peaceful purposes and science.
Penguins, seals and whales live around its coasts.

tx.t: This lecture is about the short history of the internet. The first network, ARPANET, linked four American research sites in nineteen sixty-nine.

In nineteen seventy-one, Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers and chose the at sign for addresses. Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, invented the World Wide Web at the end of the nineteen eighties.

The web and the internet are not the same thing: the internet is the network, and the web is one service that runs on it. Google was founded in nineteen ninety-eight by two students at Stanford University.
Today, more than five billion people use the internet.

Over the last decade the cost of panels has fallen by about ninety per cent. A panel usually works for about twenty-five years, although its output slowly declines.

The scheme soon met a serious problem: too few bikes in the hills. The council solved it with a van that moves bikes uphill every morning.
Today, a ride costs two pounds thirty for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.
